Earth's Space Twins: Analog Sites for Moon & Mars Bases

The Space Explorer · Team 309 orbit not found · Presented by Aaryan Anil Bhenwal

Overview

Before astronauts build permanent bases on the Moon or Mars, they must test spacesuits, rovers and habitats on Earth. The Space Explorer identifies Earth locations that are analogs of permanent Moon base sites and Mars. Using open data from NASA, our project maps Earth's best "Space Twins": extreme locations with volcanic caves, freezing deserts and ancient craters that mirror the Moon and Mars.

Why Test on Earth?

  • Test future habitats: try out Moon and Mars habitats here on Earth.
  • Find similar environments: permafrost, lava tubes and deserts.
  • Compare the data: Earth versus planetary data on geology, environment and resources.
  • Test the systems: robotics, habitats and human survival systems.

Earth analogs let us test future Moon and Mars habitats, robotics and survival systems before going to space.

Analogs cannot copy everything, so we match the conditions that matter for each test.

How It Works

The platform is a digital bridge between planetary datasets and terrestrial climate and geographic databases. We rely on cross-planetary data integration, not guesswork.

  1. Planetary data: Mars and lunar orbiters and rovers provide temperature, soil chemistry and terrain.
  2. Earth data: terrestrial climate and geographic databases.
  3. Matching algorithm: analyzes the overlapping layers in real time.
  4. Real-world coordinates: exact sites on Earth that replicate Moon and Mars conditions, where survival can be engineered and proven.

The Space Twins Map (Google Earth)

Our Google Earth project pins seven sites. Each pin records the space match, why it matches, how it would be used for a base, and its limits.

Devon Island, Canada

75.20° N, 81.85° W

Mars: polar regions and impact craters

Largest uninhabited island on Earth, with freezing temperatures, rocky permafrost and the ancient Haughton Impact Crater

Testing Mars habitats, spacesuits and rovers in extreme cold and isolation

Craters of the Moon, Idaho, USA

43.40° N, 114.03° W

Moon and Mars: volcanic plains and lava tubes

Dark basaltic lava flows, volcanic craters and underground lava caves that mirror the Moon's surface

Practicing walking on sharp volcanic rock and using caves to hide from space radiation

Meteor Crater, Arizona, USA

35.03° N, 111.02° W

Moon and Mars: fresh impact craters

Giant bowl-shaped crater from a meteorite impact, surrounded by ejected rocks and dusty soil

Learning to map craters, collect rock samples and navigate steep crater walls

Atacama Desert, Chile

23.86° S, 69.13° W

Mars: dry surface soil

Driest non-polar desert on Earth, with red, salty, iron-rich soil and almost zero rainfall

Testing rover drills that search for underground water and signs of microscopic life

Mauna Loa, Hawaii, USA

19.47° N, 155.59° W

Mars: volcanic slopes and lava fields

Massive shield volcano with red-black basalt soil and no plants at high altitudes

Closed-dome isolation missions where crews practice living and working together

Ladakh, India

34.23° N, 77.56° E

Mars: ancient lakebeds and cold deserts

Freezing, high-altitude cold desert with dry rocky valleys, salty lakes and permafrost soil

Testing habitats, rovers and human survival in thin, freezing air

Rio Tinto, Spain

37.38° N, 6.66° W

Mars: iron-rich rocks and ancient water

Bright red river packed with iron and sulfur minerals, creating rocks like those found on Mars

Testing instruments that detect ancient water and microbes inside Martian rocks

Worked Example: Martian Lava Tubes

A mission planner needs to test how an autonomous rover handles the sharp, basaltic shards of a Martian lava tube. The Space Explorer pinpoints Earth sites that replicate those physical conditions. On our map, Mauna Loa in Hawaii offers volcanic basalt terrain, and Craters of the Moon in Idaho adds underground lava caves for testing movement and radiation shelter.

Three Core Applications

  • Robotics: test how rovers and autonomous machines handle rugged, alien terrain.
  • Habitats: trial shelters and structures in environments that match Moon and Mars sites.
  • Human survival: engineer and prove life-support and crew systems before they leave Earth.

Benefits

  • Hardware and crews can be tested on Earth, which is safer and cheaper than testing in space.
  • Site selection is based on data rather than guesswork.
  • The seven sites cover different needs: extreme cold, volcanic terrain, impact craters, dry soil, crew isolation and mineral and water detection.
  • Every site lists its own limits, so teams know what an Earth test can and cannot prove.

Intended Impact

Our goal is better-prepared Moon and Mars missions. By turning abstract cosmic telemetry into actionable, real-world coordinates, the project gives space teams places where human survival can be engineered and proven before launch.

Tools and Technology

  • Google Earth: the interactive map, with placemarks and a slideshow tour of each site.
  • Google Slides: the project presentation.
  • Open NASA data: the data source behind the planetary and terrain comparisons.
  • Matching algorithm: overlays planetary and Earth data layers to find analog sites.

What Makes It Creative

Instead of looking to space for answers, the project looks at Earth. It treats the planet's most extreme places as "space twins" for the Moon and Mars. Each site is paired with an honest challenge, and the interactive map lets anyone fly to each location and see the match.

Factors We Considered

  • Differences between worlds: gravity, atmosphere, radiation, weather and life.
  • Limits of each analog:
    • Devon Island has breathable air and about three times Mars's gravity.
    • Craters of the Moon has air, wind and Earth's gravity.
    • Meteor Crater is slowly eroded by wind and rain, unlike the airless Moon.
    • The Atacama's atmosphere blocks the harsh radiation that hits the Martian surface.
    • Mauna Loa has higher air pressure and stronger gravity than Mars.
    • Ladakh has thin air, but Mars's air is much thinner and unbreathable.
    • Rio Tinto has flowing liquid water on the surface, while Mars's water is frozen underground.
  • Matching to the test: no site copies everything, so each is chosen for the conditions that matter to a specific test.
  • Variety and access: sites span several countries and environment types, from polar to desert to volcanic.

Conclusion

Earth's Space Twins maps the cosmos to Earth. By matching Moon and Mars conditions to real places, it helps robots, habitats and crews get ready for the journey before they leave the planet.
